claim: Cholesterol is necessary for the function of many G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: Cholesterol is necessary for the function of many G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs).
evidence: This is a general statement about cholesterol and GPCRs that draws on established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Cholesterol is sufficient to activate signaling by the Hedgehog (Hh) pathway.
source: We find that cholesterol is not just necessary but also sufficient to activate signaling by the Hedgehog (Hh) pathway, a prominent cell-cell communication system in development.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-5.

claim: Cholesterol influences Hh signaling by directly activating Smoothened (SMO).
source: Cholesterol influences Hh signaling by directly activating Smoothened (SMO), an orphan GPCR that transmits the Hh signal across the membrane in all animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by epistasis experiments and mutational analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: SMO is an orphan GPCR that transmits the Hh signal across the membrane in all animals.
source: Cholesterol influences Hh signaling by directly activating Smoothened (SMO), an orphan GPCR that transmits the Hh signal across the membrane in all animals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMO's role in Hedgehog signaling.

claim: SMO is activated by cholesterol through its extracellular cysteine-rich domain (CRD) rather than through its heptahelical transmembrane domain.
source: Unlike many GPCRs, which are regulated by cholesterol through their heptahelical transmembrane domains, SMO is activated by cholesterol through its extracellular cysteine-rich domain (CRD).
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis in Figure 4 showing that CRD mutations but not 7TMD mutations block cholesterol signaling.

claim: Residues that mediate cholesterol binding to the CRD also dictate SMO activation in response to cholesterol and native Hh ligands.
source: Residues shown to mediate cholesterol binding to the CRD in a recent structural analysis also dictate SMO activation, both in response to cholesterol and to native Hh ligands.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis in Figure 4 and references to structural data.

claim: Cholesterol can initiate signaling from the cell surface by engaging the extracellular domain of a GPCR.
source: Our results show that cholesterol can initiate signaling from the cell surface by engaging the extracellular domain of a GPCR and suggest that SMO activity may be regulated by local changes in cholesterol abundance or accessibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SMO activity may be regulated by local changes in cholesterol abundance or accessibility.
source: Our results show that cholesterol can initiate signaling from the cell surface by engaging the extracellular domain of a GPCR and suggest that SMO activity may be regulated by local changes in cholesterol abundance or accessibility.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Cholesterol makes up nearly half of the lipid molecules in the plasma membrane of animal cells.
source: Cholesterol, which makes up nearly half of the lipid molecules in the plasma membrane of animal cells, can influence many signal transduction events at the cell surface.
evidence: This is established knowledge about membrane composition.

claim: Cholesterol plays an important role in modulating the function of cell-surface receptors, including GPCRs and antigen receptors on immune cells.
source: It plays an important role in modulating the function of cell-surface receptors, including G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest class of receptors that transduce signals across the plasma membrane, and antigen receptors on immune cells (Burger et al., 2000; Pucadyil and Chattopadhyay, 2006; Swamy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The structures of several GPCRs reveal cholesterol molecules tightly associated with the heptahelical transmembrane domain (7TMD).
source: The structures of several GPCRs reveal cholesterol molecules tightly associated with the heptahelical transmembrane domain (7TMD) (Cherezov et al., 2007; Ruprecht et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Cholesterol can influence GPCR stability, oligomerization and ligand affinity.
source: Cholesterol can influence GPCR stability, oligomerization and ligand affinity (Fahrenholz et al., 1995; Gimpl et al., 1997; Gimpl and Fahrenholz, 2002; Prasanna et al., 2014; Pucadyil and Chattopadhyay, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cholesterol organizes membrane microdomains, or 'rafts,' containing proteins and lipids that function as platforms for the detection and propagation of extracellular signals.
source: Cholesterol also organizes membrane microdomains, or 'rafts,' containing proteins and lipids that function as platforms for the detection and propagation of extracellular signals (Lingwood and Simons, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The best-defined role for cholesterol in Hh signaling is in the biogenesis of Hh ligands.
source: While the best-defined role for cholesterol is in the biogenesis of Hh ligands (Porter et al., 1996), it also plays an independent role in the reception of Hh signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic depletion of cholesterol reduces cellular responses to Hh ligands.
source: Pharmacological or genetic depletion of cholesterol reduces cellular responses to Hh ligands, which has led to the view that cholesterol is permissive for Hh signaling (Blassberg et al., 2016; Cooper et al., 1998; Cooper et al., 2003; Incardona et al., 1998; Incardona and Roelink, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An acute increase in plasma membrane cholesterol is sufficient to activate Hh signaling.
source: Distinct from these previous observations, we find that an acute increase in plasma membrane cholesterol is sufficient to activate Hh signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol complexes are the most effective way to rapidly increase cholesterol in the plasma membrane.
source: MβCD:cholesterol complexes have been shown to be the most effective way to rapidly increase cholesterol in the plasma membrane, the subcellular location for most transmembrane signaling events (Christian et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol activated Hh signaling in NIH/3T3 cells and Mouse Embryonic Fibroblasts (MEFs).
source: MβCD:cholesterol activated Hh signaling in NIH/3T3 cells and Mouse Embryonic Fibroblasts (MEFs), cultured cell lines that have been extensively used for mechanistic studies of the Hh pathway (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol treatment activated the transcription of Gli1, a direct Hh target gene.
source: MβCD:cholesterol treatment activated the transcription of Gli1 (Figure 1A and B), a direct Hh target gene used as a measure of signal strength, and also reduced protein levels of the repressor form of the transcription factor GLI3, a consequence of signaling known to be independent of transcription (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol reduced protein levels of the repressor form of the transcription factor GLI3.
source: MβCD:cholesterol treatment activated the transcription of Gli1 (Figure 1A and B), a direct Hh target gene used as a measure of signal strength, and also reduced protein levels of the repressor form of the transcription factor GLI3, a consequence of signaling known to be independent of transcription (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol induced a concentration-dependent, bell-shaped Hh signaling response.
source: MβCD:cholesterol induced a concentration-dependent, bell-shaped Hh signaling response (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Low doses of MβCD:cholesterol increased the potency of the native ligand SHH.
source: Low doses of MβCD:cholesterol, which have only a minor effect on signaling, also increased the potency of the native ligand SHH, as seen by a leftward shift in the SHH dose-response curve (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cholesterol loading of cells by MβCD:cholesterol was nearly complete by 2 hr.
source: Cholesterol loading of cells by MβCD:cholesterol was nearly complete by 2 hr, as determined by a standard enzymatic assay for free (unesterified) cholesterol (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The increase in cellular levels of free cholesterol was confirmed by the transcriptional suppression of genes encoding enzymes in the pathway for cholesterol biosynthesis.
source: The increase in cellular levels of free cholesterol was also confirmed by the transcriptional suppression of genes encoding enzymes in the pathway for cholesterol biosynthesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was a significant increase in the accessible or chemically active pool of cholesterol in the plasma membrane after MβCD:cholesterol treatment.
source: Importantly, there was a significant increase in the accessible or chemically active (Radhakrishnan and McConnell, 2000) pool of cholesterol in the plasma membrane, as shown by increased cell-surface labeling with a cholesterol-binding toxin (Perfringolysin O (PFO), Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)(Das et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citations to prior literature.

claim: The initial activation of Gli1 by MβCD:cholesterol coincided with the loading of cells with cholesterol, starting at 2 hr.
source: The initial activation of Gli1 by MβCD:cholesterol coincided with the loading of cells with cholesterol, starting at 2 hr (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The kinetics of Gli1 induction by MβCD:cholesterol paralleled those of Gli1 induction by the native ligand SHH.
source: The kinetics of Gli1 induction by MβCD:cholesterol paralleled those of Gli1 induction by the native ligand SHH, despite the fact the absolute levels of signaling were higher in response to SHH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The rapid Hh signaling response to cholesterol is unlikely to be mediated by indirect or secondary transcriptional effects.
source: The rapid Hh signaling response to cholesterol, temporally correlated with the acute increase in cholesterol levels in the plasma membrane, is unlikely to be mediated by indirect or secondary transcriptional effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data presented.

claim: Hh signaling activity increased in proportion to the amount of cholesterol in the MβCD:cholesterol complexes when MβCD concentration was held constant.
source: Following a previously-described protocol (Christian et al., 1997), we treated fibroblasts with a series of MβCD complexes in which the MβCD concentration was held constant at 1.25 mM while the cholesterol concentration was varied. Under these conditions, Hh signaling activity increased in proportion to the amount of cholesterol in the MβCD:cholesterol complexes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cholesterol must be the active ingredient in MβCD:cholesterol complexes that activates Hh signaling.
source: Thus, cholesterol must be the active ingredient in these complexes that activates Hh signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dose-response data in Figure 2A.

claim: The Hh signaling activity of cholesterol was exquisitely stereoselective.
source: The Hh signaling activity of cholesterol was exquisitely stereoselective— neither its enantiomer (ent-cholesterol) nor an epimer with an inverted configuration only at the 3-hydroxy position (epi-cholesterol) could activate Hh target genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Enantioselectivity was consistent with cholesterol acting through a chiral binding pocket on a protein target, rather than by altering membrane properties.
source: Enantioselectivity was consistent with cholesterol acting through a chiral binding pocket on a protein target, rather than by altering membrane properties (Covey, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the stereoselectivity data and cited literature.

claim: Hh signaling activity was lost when either the number or the position of double bonds in the tetracyclic sterol nucleus were altered in 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC) and lathosterol.
source: Hh signaling activity was also lost when either the number or the position of double bonds in the tetracyclic sterol nucleus were altered in 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC) and lathosterol, two endogenous biosynthetic precursors of cholesterol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Desmosterol retained Hh signaling activity.
source: Interestingly, desmosterol, another immediate biosynthetic precursor of cholesterol that contains an additional double-bond in the iso-octyl chain, retained signaling activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The tetracyclic ring, conserved between cholesterol and desmosterol, is the critical structural element required for Hh signaling activity.
source: This structure-activity relationship points to the tetracyclic ring, conserved between cholesterol and desmosterol, as the critical structural element required for activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure-activity relationship data.

claim: The strict structural requirements suggest a specific, protein-mediated effect of cholesterol on the Hh signaling pathway.
source: These strict structural requirements suggest a specific, protein-mediated effect of cholesterol on the Hh signaling pathway and further exclude the possibility that signaling activity is due to extraction of an inhibitor from cells by MβCD (present at the same concentration in all the sterol complexes tested in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure-activity relationship data.

claim: PTCH1 inhibits signaling by suppressing the activity of SMO.
source: The receptor for Hh ligands, Patched 1 (PTCH1), inhibits signaling by suppressing the activity of SMO, a member of the GPCR superfamily.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hh signaling pathway.

claim: SHH binds and inhibits PTCH1, thereby allowing SMO to adopt an active conformation and transmit the Hh signal across the plasma membrane.
source: SHH binds and inhibits PTCH1, thereby allowing SMO to adopt an active conformation and transmit the Hh signal across the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hh signaling pathway.

claim: Forskolin blocks Hh signaling at a step between SMO and the GLI proteins.
source: The addition of forskolin (Fsk), which leads to an increase in the activity of PKA, blocks Hh signaling at a step between SMO and the GLI proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hh signaling pathway.

claim: Forskolin inhibited MβCD:cholesterol-mediated signaling, placing the site of cholesterol action at the level of or upstream of PKA.
source: Fsk inhibited MβCD:cholesterol-mediated signaling, placing the site of cholesterol action at the level of or upstream of PKA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cyclopamine and vismodegib blocked Gli1 activation by MβCD:cholesterol.
source: Two direct SMO antagonists, the steroidal natural product cyclopamine and the anti-cancer drug vismodegib, blocked Gli1 activation by MβCD:cholesterol (Figure 3B) (Sharpe et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol requires SMO activity to promote signaling.
source: This pharmacological profile established that MβCD:cholesterol requires SMO activity to promote signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological data in Figure 3B.

claim: MEFs completely lacking SMO (Smo-/- cells) failed to respond to MβCD:cholesterol.
source: Indeed, MEFs completely lacking SMO (Smo-/- cells) failed to respond to MβCD:cholesterol, and the stable re-expression of wild-type (WT) SMO, but not a point mutant locked in an inactive conformation (Smo-V333F), rescued signaling (Figure 3C) (Varjosalo et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The stable re-expression of wild-type SMO, but not a point mutant locked in an inactive conformation (Smo-V333F), rescued signaling in Smo-/- cells.
source: Indeed, MEFs completely lacking SMO (Smo-/- cells) failed to respond to MβCD:cholesterol, and the stable re-expression of wild-type (WT) SMO, but not a point mutant locked in an inactive conformation (Smo-V333F), rescued signaling (Figure 3C) (Varjosalo et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol activated signaling in Ptch1-/- cells treated with cyclopamine to partially suppress SMO activity.
source: MβCD:cholesterol activated signaling in Ptch1-/- cells treated with cyclopamine to partially suppress SMO activity, showing that cholesterol signaling activity did not depend on the presence of PTCH1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cholesterol signaling activity did not depend on the presence of PTCH1.
source: MβCD:cholesterol activated signaling in Ptch1-/- cells treated with cyclopamine to partially suppress SMO activity, showing that cholesterol signaling activity did not depend on the presence of PTCH1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol behaved much like the direct SMO agonist SAG in Ptch1-/- cells.
source: MβCD:cholesterol behaved much like the direct SMO agonist SAG, since both could overcome SMO inhibition by cyclopamine in the absence of PTCH1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SMO did not accumulate to high levels in primary cilia in cells treated with MβCD:cholesterol compared to treatment with the native ligand SHH.
source: However, compared to treatment with the native ligand SHH, SMO did not accumulate to high levels in primary cilia in cells treated with MβCD:cholesterol (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), an observation that may explain the lower signaling efficacy of cholesterol compared to SHH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: SMO contains two physically separable binding sites capable of interacting with steroidal ligands.
source: SMO contains two physically separable binding sites capable of interacting with steroidal ligands (Figure 4A) (Nachtergaele et al., 2012; Sharpe et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and structural data.

claim: Agonistic oxysterols, such as 20(S)-hydroxycholesterol (20(S)-OHC), engage a hydrophobic groove on the surface of the extracellular cysteine-rich domain (CRD) of SMO.
source: Agonistic oxysterols, such as 20(S)-hydroxycholesterol (20(S)-OHC), engage a hydrophobic groove on the surface of the extracellular cysteine-rich domain (CRD) of SMO (Myers et al., 2013; Nachtergaele et al., 2013; Nedelcu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cholesterol could occupy the CRD groove of SMO.
source: We recently reported that cholesterol could also occupy this CRD groove (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: A cholesterol molecule was resolved in the CRD groove in a crystal structure of SMO.
source: A cholesterol molecule was resolved in this groove in a crystal structure of SMO.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from prior work.

claim: Purified SMO bound to beads covalently coupled to cholesterol and this interaction could be blocked by free 20(S)-OHC.
source: Furthermore, purified SMO bound to beads covalently coupled to cholesterol and this interaction could be blocked by free 20(S)-OHC, consistent with the view that both 20(S)-OHC and cholesterol occupy the same binding site (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The extracellular end of the SMO 7TMD binds to the steroidal alkaloid cyclopamine, as well as to several non-steroidal synthetic agonists and antagonists.
source: In addition, the extracellular end of the SMO 7TMD binds to the steroidal alkaloid cyclopamine, as well as to several non-steroidal synthetic agonists and antagonists (Chen et al., 2002a; Chen et al., 2002b; Frank-Kamenetsky et al., 2002; Khaliullina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Asp477Gly mutation in the 7TM binding-site of SMO reduces binding and responsiveness to a subset of 7TM ligands, including SAG and vismodegib.
source: The Asp477Gly mutation in the 7TM binding-site of SMO (Figure 4A), initially isolated from a patient whose tumor had become resistant to vismodegib, reduces binding and responsiveness to a subset of 7TM ligands, including SAG and vismodegib (Yauch et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Asp99Ala/Tyr134Phe and Gly115Phe are mutations at opposite ends of the shallow sterol-binding groove in the CRD that block the ability of 20(S)-OHC to both bind SMO and activate Hh signaling.
source: In the CRD, Asp99Ala/Tyr134Phe and Gly115Phe are mutations at opposite ends of the shallow sterol-binding groove that block the ability of 20(S)-OHC to both bind SMO and activate Hh signaling (Figure 4A) (Nachtergaele et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Asp99Ala and Tyr134Phe mutations disrupt a hydrogen-bonding network with the 3β-hydroxyl group of sterols.
source: The Asp99Ala and Tyr134Phe mutations disrupt a hydrogen-bonding network with the 3β-hydroxyl group of sterols (Figure 4A, inset) (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors and structural data.

claim: The Asp477Gly mutation in the 7TMD domain had no effect on the ability of MβCD:cholesterol to activate Hh signaling.
source: The Asp477Gly mutation in the 7TMD domain had no effect on the ability of MβCD:cholesterol to activate Hh signaling (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: SMO bearing a bulkier, charge-reversed mutation at the Asp477 site (Asp477Arg) that increases constitutive signaling activity remained responsive to MβCD:cholesterol.
source: SMO bearing a bulkier, charge-reversed mutation at this site (Asp477Arg) that increases constitutive signaling activity also remained responsive to MβCD:cholesterol (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) (Dijkgraaf et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Asp99Ala/Tyr134Phe mutation in the CRD reduced the ability of MβCD:cholesterol to activate Hh signaling.
source: In contrast, the Asp99Ala/Tyr134Phe mutation in the CRD reduced the ability of MβCD:cholesterol to activate Hh signaling (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Asp99Ala/Tyr134Phe SMO mutant was impaired in its responsiveness to SHH and to 20(S)-OHC, but remained responsive to the 7TMD ligand SAG.
source: The Asp99Ala/Tyr134Phe SMO mutant was also impaired in its responsiveness to SHH and to 20(S)-OHC, but remained responsive to the 7TMD ligand SAG (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A complete deletion of the CRD (SMO-△CRD) abolished signaling responses to MβCD:cholesterol.
source: A complete deletion of the CRD (SMO-△CRD), which increased basal SMO signaling activity like the Asp477Arg mutation, also abolished signaling responses to MβCD:cholesterol (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) (Myers et al., 2013; Nedelcu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The CRD binding-site, rather than the 7TMD binding-site, mediates the effect of cholesterol on SMO activity and thus on Hh signaling.
source: This mutational analysis supports the model that the CRD binding-site, rather than the 7TMD binding-site, mediates the effect of cholesterol on SMO activity and thus on Hh signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data in Figure 4.

claim: A mutation in Gly115 did not alter the response to MβCD:cholesterol, even though it diminished the response to 20(S)-OHC.
source: Interestingly, a mutation in Gly115, which is located on the opposite end of the CRD ligand-binding groove (Figure 4A), did not alter the response to MβCD:cholesterol, even though it diminished the response to 20(S)-OHC as previously noted (Figure 4D) (Nachtergaele et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The SMO-Gly115Phe mutant responded normally to the native ligand SHH.
source: The SMO-Gly115Phe mutant also responded normally to the native ligand SHH (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The ability of mutations to segregate 20(S)-OHC responses from cholesterol responses is consistent with solution-state small-angle X-Ray scattering data showing distinct conformations for SMO bound to these two steroidal ligands.
source: The ability of mutations to segregate 20(S)-OHC responses from cholesterol responses is consistent with solution-state small-angle X-Ray scattering data showing distinct conformations for SMO bound to these two steroidal ligands (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: 20(S)-OHC, 25-OHC and 27-OHC were all significantly compromised in their ability to activate Hh signaling in cells expressing SMO-Gly115Phe.
source: However, 20(S)-OHC, 25-OHC and 27-OHC, when delivered to cells as MβCD conjugates, were all significantly compromised in their ability to activate Hh signaling in cells expressing SMO-Gly115Phe (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cholesterol-induced signaling was unaffected by the Gly115Phe mutation.
source: In contrast, cholesterol-induced signaling was unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D); therefore, cholesterol must not be activating signaling by being metabolized to one of these side-chain oxysterols.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cholesterol must not be activating signaling by being metabolized to side-chain oxysterols.
source: In contrast, cholesterol-induced signaling was unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D); therefore, cholesterol must not be activating signaling by being metabolized to one of these side-chain oxysterols.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of the Gly115Phe mutation on cholesterol versus oxysterol signaling.

claim: Cholesterol can directly activate Hh signaling through the CRD of SMO.
source: Instead, our data suggests that cholesterol can directly activate Hh signaling through the CRD of SMO.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol induced the formation of both Nkx6.1+ and Olig2+ progenitor subtypes at a low frequency in cultures of mouse spinal cord progenitors.
source: MβCD:cholesterol induced the formation of both Nkx6.1+ and Olig2+ progenitor subtypes at a low frequency in cultures of mouse spinal cord progenitors (Figure 5B and C) and also activated the transcription of Gli1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol activated the transcription of Gli1 in mouse spinal cord progenitors.
source: MβCD:cholesterol induced the formation of both Nkx6.1+ and Olig2+ progenitor subtypes at a low frequency in cultures of mouse spinal cord progenitors (Figure 5B and C) and also activated the transcription of Gli1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The activation of both Gli1 induction and ventral neural specification by MβCD:cholesterol was significantly less than that produced by a saturating concentration of SHH.
source: The activation of both Gli1 induction and ventral neural specification by MβCD:cholesterol was significantly less than that produced by a saturating concentration of SHH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol is sufficient to activate low-level Hh signals in neural progenitors and consequently to direct differentiation towards neural cell types that depend on such signals.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that MβCD:cholesterol is sufficient to activate low-level Hh signals in neural progenitors and consequently to direct differentiation towards neural cell types that depend on such signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural differentiation data in Figure 5.

claim: Cholesterol has been shown to be necessary for SMO activation, based on experiments using inhibitors of cholesterol biosynthesis and high concentrations of naked MβCD to strip the plasma membrane of cholesterol.
source: Cholesterol has been shown to be necessary for SMO activation, based on experiments using inhibitors of cholesterol biosynthesis and high concentrations of naked MβCD to strip the plasma membrane of cholesterol (Cooper et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Impaired SMO activation caused by cholesterol deficiency has been noted in Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS), a congenital malformation syndrome caused by defects in the enzyme that converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholesterol.
source: Impaired SMO activation caused by cholesterol deficiency has also been noted in Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS), a congenital malformation syndrome caused by defects in the enzyme that converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholesterol (Blassberg et al., 2016; Cooper et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The SMO CRD is dispensable for the permissive role of cholesterol.
source: In contrast to our results, the SMO CRD is dispensable for this permissive role of cholesterol.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The depletion of cholesterol reduces signaling by SMO mutants lacking the entire CRD or carrying mutations in the CRD binding-groove.
source: The depletion of cholesterol reduces signaling by SMO mutants lacking the entire CRD (Myers et al., 2013) or carrying mutations in the CRD binding-groove (Blassberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The permissive effects of cholesterol are likely to be mediated by the SMO 7TMD, by analogy with other GPCRs.
source: By analogy with other GPCRs, these permissive effects are likely to be mediated by the SMO 7TMD.
evidence: This is an inference based on analogy with other GPCRs.

claim: Cholesterol engages a hydrophobic groove on the surface of the CRD, a groove that was previously shown to mediate the activating influence of oxysterols.
source: This instructive effect is mediated by the Class F GPCR SMO and maps to its extracellular CRD. Cholesterol engages a hydrophobic groove on the surface of the CRD, a groove that was previously shown to mediate the activating influence of oxysterols (Myers et al., 2013; Nachtergaele et al., 2013; Nedelcu et al., 2013) and represents an evolutionarily conserved mechanism for detecting hydrophobic small-molecule ligands (Bazan and de Sauvage, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and structural data.

claim: The CRD groove represents an evolutionarily conserved mechanism for detecting hydrophobic small-molecule ligands.
source: Cholesterol engages a hydrophobic groove on the surface of the CRD, a groove that was previously shown to mediate the activating influence of oxysterols (Myers et al., 2013; Nachtergaele et al., 2013; Nedelcu et al., 2013) and represents an evolutionarily conserved mechanism for detecting hydrophobic small-molecule ligands (Bazan and de Sauvage, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: An analogous mechanism is present in the Frizzled family of Wnt receptors, where the Frizzled CRD binds to the palmitoleyl group of Wnt ligands, an interaction that is required for Wnt signaling.
source: An analogous mechanism is present in the Frizzled family of Wnt receptors, where the Frizzled CRD binds to the palmitoleyl group of Wnt ligands, an interaction that is required for Wnt signaling (Janda et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The instructive effects of cholesterol and the permissive effects of cholesterol map to distinct, separable SMO domains.
source: Thus, the instructive effects of cholesterol revealed in our present study and the permissive effects of cholesterol reported previously map to distinct, separable SMO domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of the current findings with prior literature.

claim: The observation that MβCD:cholesterol is sufficient to activate SMO through its CRD is in agreement with a report published recently during the review process of the manuscript.
source: Our observation that MβCD:cholesterol is sufficient to activate SMO through its CRD is in agreement with a report published recently during the review process of our manuscript (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a concurrent publication.

claim: The method of delivery, as an inclusion complex with MβCD, is critical to presenting cholesterol in a bioavailable form capable of activating Smo.
source: First, the method of delivery, as an inclusion complex with MβCD, is critical to presenting cholesterol, a profoundly hydrophobic and insoluble lipid, in a bioavailable form capable of activating Smo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental approach and the properties of cholesterol.

claim: Side-chain oxysterols are significantly more hydrophilic and soluble in aqueous solutions than cholesterol, shown by their ~ 50 fold faster transfer rates between membranes.
source: In contrast, side-chain oxysterols, which harbor an additional hydroxyl group, are significantly more hydrophilic and soluble in aqueous solutions, shown by their ~ 50 fold faster transfer rates between membranes (Theunissen et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cholesterol levels in the cell are tightly controlled by elaborate homeostatic signalling mechanisms.
source: Second, cholesterol levels in the cell are difficult to manipulate because they are tightly controlled by elaborate homeostatic signalling mechanisms (Brown and Goldstein, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol inclusion complexes are unique in their ability to increase the cholesterol content of the plasma membrane rapidly at timescales (~1–4 hr) at which cytoplasmic signaling pathways operate.
source: MβCD:cholesterol inclusion complexes have been shown to be unique in their ability to increase the cholesterol content of the plasma membrane rapidly at timescales (~1–4 hr) at which cytoplasmic signaling pathways operate (Christian et al., 1997; Yancey et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The bell-shaped Hh signal-response curve implies that MβCD:cholesterol must be delivered in a relatively narrow, intermediate concentration range (1–2 mM) to observe optimal activity.
source: Finally, the bell-shaped Hh signal-response curve (Figure 1A) implies that MβCD:cholesterol must be delivered in a relatively narrow, intermediate concentration range (1–2 mM) to observe optimal activity, with higher (>5 mM) concentrations commonly used to load cells with cholesterol producing markedly lower levels of signaling activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dose-response data in Figure 1A.

claim: SMO△C was unexpectedly found to contain a cholesterol ligand in its CRD groove.
source: SMO△C was unexpectedly found to contain a cholesterol ligand in its CRD groove.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior structural work.

claim: Cholesterol made key contacts with the linker domain and third extracellular loop of the 7TMD in the SMO structure.
source: Cholesterol also made key contacts with the linker domain and third extracellular loop of the 7TMD (Figure 4A), and molecular dynamics simulations showed that cholesterol can stabilize these extracellular regions of SMO (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior structural work.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations showed that cholesterol can stabilize the extracellular regions of SMO.
source: Cholesterol also made key contacts with the linker domain and third extracellular loop of the 7TMD (Figure 4A), and molecular dynamics simulations showed that cholesterol can stabilize these extracellular regions of SMO (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior computational work.

claim: Structure-guided point mutations in CRD residues that form hydrogen-bonding interactions with the 3β-hydroxyl of cholesterol reduced signaling by cholesterol.
source: Structure-guided point mutations in CRD residues that form hydrogen-bonding interactions with the 3β-hydroxyl of cholesterol, reduced signaling by cholesterol (Figure 4C), making it likely that cholesterol activates SMO by binding to the CRD in the pose revealed in the structure (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cholesterol activates SMO by binding to the CRD in the pose revealed in the structure.
source: Structure-guided point mutations in CRD residues that form hydrogen-bonding interactions with the 3β-hydroxyl of cholesterol, reduced signaling by cholesterol (Figure 4C), making it likely that cholesterol activates SMO by binding to the CRD in the pose revealed in the structure (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutational analysis and structural data.

claim: The cholesterol-bound SMO structure may represent an active-state conformation of the CRD.
source: Thus, the cholesterol-bound SMO structure recently reported by our groups may very well represent an active-state conformation of the CRD.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the functional and structural data.

claim: Cholesterol binding is predicted to induce a clockwise rotation of the CRD on the 7TMD pedestal, perhaps driving SMO activation by a rearrangement of contacts between the CRD and the 7TMD.
source: Cholesterol binding is predicted to induce a clockwise rotation of the CRD on the 7TMD pedestal, perhaps driving SMO activation by a rearrangement of contacts between the CRD and the 7TMD.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on structural comparisons.

claim: All structures of the SMO CRD (with the exception of the Xenopus apo-CRD) are conformationally identical, regardless of whether they contain a bound ligand or not.
source: Second, all structures of the SMO CRD (with the exception of the Xenopus apo-CRD) are conformationally identical (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), regardless of whether they contain a bound ligand (cholesterol-bound SMO△C, cyclopamine-bound CRD or 20(S)-OHC-bound CRD) or not (Danio rerio apo-CRD or vismodegib-bound SMO△C) and regardless of whether they were crystallized by standard vapor diffusion (the CRD structures) or lipidic cubic phase methods (the SMO△C structures).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparisons shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The conserved conformation seen in both the isolated CRD and the more physiological SMO△C molecule is unlikely to be an artefact of crystal packing.
source: Hence this conserved conformation, seen in both the isolated CRD and the more physiological SMO△C molecule, is unlikely to be an artefact of crystal packing as suggested by these authors (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and a rebuttal to a claim in another publication.

claim: The region of the proposed conformational change in the Xenopus apo-SMO structure is partially disordered and involved in the coordination of a zinc ion together with a symmetry-related molecule in the crystal.
source: Finally, a careful inspection of the crystal lattice contacts in the Xenopus apo-SMO structure (PDB ID 5KZZ) revealed that the region of the proposed conformational change is partially disordered (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and involved in the coordination of a zinc ion together with a symmetry-related molecule in the crystal, a very tight, near-covalent interaction that was likely driving crystal formation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The altered conformation observed in the Xenopus apo-SMO structure may have been induced by a non-physiological, zinc-promoted crystal contact.
source: Since the crystallization solution for the Xenopus apo-SMO, but not the solutions used to crystallize the sterol-bound CRDs, contained 200 mM zinc acetate, the altered conformation observed may have been induced by a non-physiological, zinc-promoted crystal contact (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystallization conditions and structural analysis.

claim: CRD-bound cholesterol is located at a considerable distance (~12 Å) away from the membrane.
source: A surprising feature of the structure is that CRD-bound cholesterol is located at a considerable distance (~12 Å) away from the membrane, which would require a cholesterol molecule to desolvate from the membrane and become exposed to water in order to access its CRD binding pocket (Byrne et al., 2016) (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and a citation to prior work.

claim: The kinetic barrier, or the activation energy (ΔG‡) for cholesterol transfer between two acceptors through an aqueous environment is predicted to be high (~20 kcal/mole).
source: The kinetic barrier, or the activation energy (ΔG‡) for this transfer reaction is predicted to be high (~20 kcal/mole), based on the ΔG‡ for cholesterol transfer between two acceptors through an aqueous environment (Yancey et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on cholesterol transfer kinetics.

claim: The unique ability of MβCD to shield cholesterol from water while allowing its rapid transfer to acceptors would allow it to bypass the kinetically unfavorable step by delivering it to the CRD binding site.
source: The unique ability of MβCD to shield cholesterol from water while allowing its rapid transfer to acceptors would allow it to bypass this kinetically unfavorable step by delivering it to the CRD binding site (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of MβCD and the structural data.

claim: MβCD:cholesterol was consistently less active than the native ligand SHH in the assays.
source: MβCD:cholesterol was consistently less active than the native ligand SHH in our assays (Figures 1D, 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D, 5C and D.

claim: Mutations in the 7TMD binding-site do not alter the constitutive or SHH-induced signaling activity of SMO.
source: Mutations in the 7TMD binding-site do not alter the constitutive or SHH-induced signaling activity of SMO, which has led to view that this site does not regulate physiological signaling (Myers et al., 2013; Yauch et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutations in the cholesterol-binding site impaired responses to SHH.
source: In contrast, mutations in the cholesterol-binding site impaired responses to SHH (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: SMO activity is likely to be highly sensitive to both the abundance and the accessibility of cholesterol in its membrane environment.
source: The necessity and sufficiency of cholesterol for SMO activation, mediated through two different regions of the molecule, means that SMO activity is likely to be highly sensitive to both the abundance and the accessibility of cholesterol in its membrane environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings about cholesterol's role in SMO activation.

claim: PTCH1 has homology to a lysosomal cholesterol transporter, the Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) protein.
source: Furthermore, PTCH1 has homology to a lysosomal cholesterol transporter, the Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) protein (Carstea et al., 1997), and PTCH1 has been purported to have cholesterol binding and transport activity (Bidet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PTCH1 has been purported to have cholesterol binding and transport activity.
source: Furthermore, PTCH1 has homology to a lysosomal cholesterol transporter, the Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) protein (Carstea et al., 1997), and PTCH1 has been purported to have cholesterol binding and transport activity (Bidet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PTCH1 may inhibit SMO by reducing cholesterol content or cholesterol accessibility in a membrane compartment that also contains SMO.
source: Thus, our work supports a model where PTCH1 may inhibit SMO by reducing cholesterol content or cholesterol accessibility (or chemical activity) in a membrane compartment that also contains SMO, leading to alterations in SMO conformation or trafficking (Bidet et al., 2011; Incardona et al., 2002; Khaliullina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative model supported by the findings and citations to prior literature.

claim: PTCH1-induced changes in cholesterol are likely to be confined to a specific membrane compartment.
source: Since cholesterol is a ubiquitous component of cellular membranes that affects many cellular processes, PTCH1-induced changes in cholesterol are likely to be confined to a specific membrane compartment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of cholesterol and cellular organization.

claim: The base of the cilium is a good candidate for a compartment where PTCH1-induced changes in cholesterol occur.
source: The base of the cilium is a good candidate for such a compartment because PTCH1 is localized most prominently at the ciliary base in Hh-responsive tissues in the mouse embryo (Rohatgi et al., 2007) and because most Hh pathway components, from PTCH1 to the GLI transcription factors, are found in and around primary cilia (Briscoe and Thérond, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal supported by citations to prior literature on PTCH1 localization and Hh pathway components.

claim: Cholesterol may be used as a second messenger to instruct signaling events at the cell surface through GPCRs and perhaps other cell-surface receptors.
source: While cholesterol is an abundant lipid, clearly critical for maintaining membrane biophysical properties and for stabilizing membrane proteins, our work suggests that it may be also used as a second messenger to instruct signaling events at the cell surface through GPCRs and perhaps other cell-surface receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the manuscript.
